# Calculating F and checking the model {.unnumbered}

```{r}
#| include: false
source("R/booktem_setup.R")
source("R/my_setup.R")
library(tidyverse)
library(webexercises)
library(here)
```

This page summarises what we covered in the first hour of the ANOVA
session, which was done on paper (students with an agreed adjustment
used a computer). Use it for revision; the full activities were worked
through in class. The computer work in Posit Cloud is in the second
hour. Each student worked on a card of their own data, so the worked
example below uses a different data set.

**Progression:** split the variation → compare signal with noise →
F = MS group ÷ MS residual → check that the residuals behave.

## From a line to group means {#sec-anova-groups}

Last week the fitted values lay on a line, and the sum of squared
residuals (SSR) measured how far the points were from it. This week the
predictor is a group label, so the fitted value for every observation is
its group mean. The residual is still observed minus fitted.

@fig-anova-illus shows 12 observations in three groups. The dashed line
is the grand mean, the mean of all 12 values.

```{r}
#| label: fig-anova-illus
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: "Twelve observations in three groups. Solid lines are the group means (10, 14 and 18). The dashed line is the grand mean (14)."

illus <- tibble(
  group_id = rep(1:3, each = 4),
  y = c(8, 10, 11, 11, 12, 14, 15, 15, 16, 18, 18, 20)
) |>
  group_by(group_id) |>
  mutate(group_mean = mean(y)) |>
  ungroup()

grand_mean <- mean(illus$y)

ggplot(illus, aes(x = group_id, y = y)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = grand_mean, linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_segment(aes(x = group_id - 0.3, xend = group_id + 0.3,
                   y = group_mean, yend = group_mean),
               colour = "steelblue", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(position = position_jitter(width = 0.1, height = 0, seed = 1),
             size = 2) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1:3,
                     labels = c("Group 1", "Group 2", "Group 3")) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Response")
```

For the highest point in Group 3 (y = 20), the distance from the grand
mean splits into two parts: 4 from the grand mean to the group mean
(18 − 14), and 2 from the group mean to the point (20 − 18). Together
they make the total distance of 6.

::: {.callout-note}
## The rule
Every observation's distance from the grand mean splits into the part
explained by its group (group mean − grand mean) and the residual
(observation − group mean). Squaring these distances and adding them
over all observations gives SS total = SS group + SS residual. SS
residual is last week's SSR, the sum of squared residuals. This session
writes SS residual so that it is not confused with "sum of squares for
regression", which some books also abbreviate to SSR.
:::

## The sums of squares by hand {#sec-anova-ss}

Each student copied the 12 values of their card into a table with four
columns: y − grand mean and its square, and y − group mean and its
square. The two squared columns add up to SS total and SS residual. SS
group is the difference. A check on the arithmetic is that the residuals
(y − group mean) add up to zero within each group.

For the data in @fig-anova-illus:

| Quantity    | Calculation                                          | Value |
|-------------|------------------------------------------------------|-------|
| SS total    | sum of (y − 14)² over all 12 observations            | 148   |
| SS residual | sum of (y − group mean)² within the three groups: 6 + 6 + 8 | 20 |
| SS group    | SS total − SS residual                               | 128   |

## From sums of squares to F {#sec-anova-f}

Each sum of squares is divided by its degrees of freedom to give a mean
square. For $k = 3$ groups and $N = 12$ observations, the group has
$k - 1 = 2$ degrees of freedom and the residual has $N - k = 9$.

| Source   | df | SS  | MS   | F    |
|----------|----|-----|------|------|
| Group    | 2  | 128 | 64   | 28.8 |
| Residual | 9  | 20  | 2.22 |      |
| Total    | 11 | 148 |      |      |

F = 64 ÷ 2.22 = 28.8, and R² = 128 ÷ 148 = 0.87. @fig-anova-fdist shows
how F behaves when the null hypothesis is true. The critical value for
these degrees of freedom is 4.26, so F = 28.8 lies far in the right-hand
tail and the p-value is about 0.0001.

```{r}
#| label: fig-anova-fdist
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: "The F-distribution with 2 and 9 degrees of freedom. The shaded area to the right of the dashed line is 5% of the distribution."

crit <- qf(0.95, df1 = 2, df2 = 9)

tibble(f = seq(0, 10, length.out = 400)) |>
  mutate(density = df(f, df1 = 2, df2 = 9)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = f, y = density)) +
  geom_area(data = ~ filter(.x, f >= crit), fill = "darkorange", alpha = 0.4) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_vline(xintercept = crit, linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(x = "F", y = "Density")
```

::: {.callout-note}
## The rule
F = MS group ÷ MS residual: the variation between the group means
(signal) divided by the variation within the groups (noise). If the
group means differ only by chance, F is usually close to 1. The p-value
is the area to the right of F in an F-distribution with k − 1 and N − k
degrees of freedom. R² = SS group ÷ SS total, and means the same as it
did in last week's regression. A significant F says that at least one
group mean differs. It does not say which one. With two groups, F is
exactly the square of the t statistic from a t-test that pools the
variance.
:::

::: {.webex-check .webex-box}
**Check your understanding.** $MS_{group}$ is 50 and $MS_{residual}$ is
5. F is `r fitb(10)`. A study has 4 groups of 6 observations each. The
group degrees of freedom are `r fitb(3)` and the residual degrees of
freedom are `r fitb(20)`.
:::

## Checking the model {#sec-anova-checks}

Last week you used a residual plot to check whether a straight line was
adequate. The same residuals are used here. Because every fitted value
is a group mean, the residual plot for an ANOVA shows one vertical
stripe of points for each group. Students sketched their own residuals,
then matched four diagnostic plots, similar to those in
@fig-anova-resid and @fig-anova-qq, to the assumption each checks.

```{r}
#| label: fig-anova-resid
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: "Residuals against fitted values for two simulated data sets. P: similar spread in every group. Q: spread increasing with the fitted value."

set.seed(21)

stripes <- tibble(
  fitted = rep(rep(c(15, 21, 27), each = 9), 2),
  plot = rep(c("Plot P", "Plot Q"), each = 27),
  residual = c(rnorm(27, 0, 1.4),
               rnorm(27, 0, rep(c(0.6, 1.8, 3.4), each = 9)))
)

ggplot(stripes, aes(x = fitted, y = residual)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", colour = "firebrick") +
  geom_point() +
  facet_wrap(~ plot) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(15, 21, 27)) +
  labs(x = "Fitted value (group mean)", y = "Residual")
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-anova-qq
#| echo: false
#| fig-cap: "Normal QQ plots for two simulated data sets. R: points follow the line, so the residuals are roughly normal. S: points curve away from the line at the upper end, so the residuals are skewed."

qq_data <- tibble(
  plot = rep(c("Plot R", "Plot S"), each = 30),
  residual = c(rnorm(30), rexp(30) - 1)
)

ggplot(qq_data, aes(sample = residual)) +
  stat_qq() +
  stat_qq_line(colour = "firebrick", linetype = "dashed") +
  facet_wrap(~ plot, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(x = "Theoretical quantile", y = "Sample quantile")
```

::: {.callout-note}
## The rule
A one-way ANOVA assumes that the residuals are roughly normally
distributed (check with a QQ plot), that the spread of the residuals is
similar in every group (check with residuals against fitted values), and
that the observations are independent (this comes from the design, not
from a plot). A check for a straight line is not needed when the only
predictor is a group label, because each group has its own mean. With
few observations, plots are hard to read.
:::

::: {.webex-check .webex-box}
**Check your understanding.** Which plot in the figures above suggests
that the spread of the residuals is not the same in every group?
`r mcq(c("Plot P", answer = "Plot Q", "Plot R", "Plot S"))`

Which assumption cannot be checked from either kind of plot?
`r mcq(c("Normal residuals", "Equal spread in every group", answer = "Independent observations"))`
:::

## Exit ticket {#sec-anova-exit}

The question posed at the end of the hour:

> Two experiments have identical group means. In experiment 2 the
> standard deviation within every group is twice as large as in
> experiment 1. By what factor does F change? Explain in one or two
> sentences.
